Oral medicine and dentistry · published research

Dental implant stability

Some studies report early stability, healing, or inflammation benefits, while other randomized comparisons and reviews find no consistent advantage. Long-term implant survival is not established.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Some studies report early stability, healing, or inflammation benefits, while other randomized comparisons and reviews find no consistent advantage. Long-term implant survival is not established.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact category contains 47 records: 26 human clinical reports, 11 animal studies, and 10 reviews, systematic reviews, or meta-analyses. Reviews synthesize overlapping primary trials, so records are not treated as 47 independent cohorts. No in-vitro/ex-vivo study is listed.

Human and clinical evidence

Findings are mixed. Some trials report improved early stability, healing, or bone measures, while others find no significant difference; meta-analyses also report inconsistent effects across time points. Protocols, populations, and implant outcomes vary, limiting a single efficacy conclusion (Camolesi et al., 2022; Arshad et al., 2024; Singhania et al., 2025). The outcomes are not interchangeable: implant stability quotient, radiographic density, bone-to-implant contact, soft-tissue healing, and marginal bone loss are measured at different follow-up intervals. Reports also differ by implant context and co-intervention. A favorable early stability result cannot be assumed to indicate long-term osseointegration or fewer implant failures; the database does not establish a common effect across these endpoints.

Primary original studies: Camolesi et al. 2023 Shenoy et al. 2024

Animal evidence

Most models report greater bone formation or osseointegration, but null results also occur, including a sheep sinus-graft experiment (Gomes et al., 2015; Jakse et al., 2007).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

none identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Camolesi et al. used combined 630 nm visible red light for mucosa and 808 nm near-infrared light for bone, with sessions immediately after surgery and 7 days later. 808 nm is outside visible light. The study did not show a clear implant-stability difference but reported healing and inflammation signals. Other protocols vary, so settings are not interchangeable.

Interpretation

Implant stability quotient, radiographic density, bone-to-implant contact, soft-tissue healing, and marginal bone loss are different outcomes measured at different times. Improvement in early healing cannot be assumed to mean durable osseointegration or fewer failures. Reviews should be counted as syntheses, not as additional clinical cohorts.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow. Human implant-stability and healing findings are mixed, and review articles overlap.
Publications and records47 unique titles.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The category contains many human studies but also animal experiments and reviews that reuse primary trials. Clinical findings differ by stability measure, follow-up, implant setting, and protocol. Some reports show early healing or stability signals, while others find no stability difference. These outcomes do not establish long-term implant survival or a common treatment effect.
